title: Human Factors in Lighting Second edition
review_question: What are the human factors in lighting, including fundamentals of light and vision, general effects on work, discomfort, and perception, and specific applications in various contexts?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not applicable for a textbook/narrative review.

findings.antecedent: human visual system
findings.consequent: responds to electromagnetic spectrum between 380 and 780 nm
findings.quote: What differentiates this wavelength range from the rest of the electromagnetic spectrum is that the human visual system responds to it.

findings.antecedent: appropriate spectral sensitivity curve
findings.consequent: derivation of luminous flux, luminous intensity, illuminance, and luminance
findings.quote: Using the appropriate spectral sensitivity curve, the four basic photometric quantities can be derived – luminous flux, luminous intensity, illuminance, and luminance.

findings.antecedent: CIE colorimetric system
findings.consequent: quantification of color appearance and color rendering properties of light sources (CCT, CRI)
findings.quote: By using these measures, colors can be quantified and the color appearance and color rendering properties of light sources characterized, using such measures as correlated color temperature and CIE General CRI.

findings.antecedent: numerous metrics for lighting situation/light source
findings.consequent: simultaneously precise and inaccurate for quantifying visual effect
findings.quote: It is important to appreciate that while there are numerous metrics used to characterize a lighting situation or a light source, these metrics are simultaneously precise and inaccurate.

findings.antecedent: visual system
findings.consequent: operates over a wide range of luminances (sunlight to starlight) by continually adjusting sensitivity
findings.quote: The visual system can operate over a wide range of luminances, from sunlight to starlight. To do this it continually adjusts its sensitivity to light, increasing its sensitivity as the amount of light available falls.

findings.antecedent: decreasing amount of light (daylight to darkness)
findings.consequent: visual system transitions through photopic, mesopic, and scotopic states
findings.quote: Decreasing the amount of light from daylight to darkness, takes the visual system through three distinct operating states, the photopic, the mesopic, and the scotopic.

findings.antecedent: scotopic conditions
findings.consequent: color not perceived, detail impossible to discriminate, fovea is blind
findings.quote: In the scotopic, the ability to make these discriminations deteriorates so that by the time the scotopic is reached, color can no longer be seen, detail is impossible to discriminate and the fovea is blind.

findings.antecedent: lighting conditions that provide enough light with wide spectral distribution and clear understanding of space
findings.consequent: lightness, color, size, and shape of objects remain constant (perceptual constancies)
findings.quote: Given lighting conditions that provide enough light with a wide spectral distribution in such a way that how the space is lit can be easily understood, the lightness, color, size, and shape of objects in the space remain constant no matter how they are viewed.

findings.antecedent: light-dark cycle
findings.consequent: entrainment of human circadian system
findings.quote: The light–dark cycle is one of the most potent of these external stimuli used for entrainment.

findings.antecedent: varying amount and timing of light exposure
findings.consequent: shift phase of circadian system clock (forward or backward)
findings.quote: by varying the amount of light exposure and when it is presented, it is possible to shift the phase of the circadian system clock, either forward or backward, as required.

findings.antecedent: light exposure at night
findings.consequent: immediate alerting effect
findings.quote: it is also possible to have an immediate alerting effect at night by exposure to light.

findings.antecedent: spectral sensitivity of retinal photoreceptor for circadian system
findings.consequent: different from CIE Standard Photopic Observer
findings.quote: it is unfortunately also true that the spectral sensitivity of the retinal photoreceptor that provides a signal to the internal oscillator is not the same as the CIE Standard Photopic Observer...

findings.antecedent: lighting conditions
findings.consequent: task performance
findings.quote: Lighting conditions can affect task performance through three systems, the visual system, the circadian system, and the perceptual system.

findings.antecedent: increasing illuminance
findings.consequent: visual performance
findings.quote: increasing illuminance follows a law of diminishing returns, i.e. that equal increments in illuminance lead to smaller and smaller changes in visual performance until saturation occurs

findings.antecedent: visually difficult task
findings.consequent: cannot reach same level of performance as visually easy task by only increasing illuminance
findings.quote: it is not possible to make a visually difficult task reach the same level of performance as a visually easy task simply by increasing the illuminance over any reasonable range.

findings.antecedent: prolonged work in inappropriate lighting conditions
findings.consequent: fatigue and mood changes
findings.quote: the possibility of other phenomena occurring if work is prolonged. These phenomena are eyestrain, fatigue, and mood changes, all of which may change task performance.

findings.antecedent: visual task difficulty, under/over-stimulation, distraction, perceptual confusion
findings.consequent: visual discomfort
findings.quote: Where lighting is intended to facilitate the extraction of information from the visual environment, there are four situations in which visual discomfort is likely to occur: visual task difficulty, under- or over-stimulation, distraction, perceptual confusion.

findings.antecedent: too little/too much light, too much illuminance variation, disability glare, discomfort glare, veiling reflections, shadows, flicker
findings.consequent: visual discomfort
findings.quote: The aspects of lighting that can cause visual discomfort are too little light, too much light, too much variation in illuminance between and across working surfaces, disability glare, discomfort glare, veiling reflections, shadows, and flicker.

findings.antecedent: luminance decreases
findings.consequent: lightness of a surface
findings.quote: as the luminance decreases, the lightness of a surface decreases.

findings.antecedent: increasing luminance of room surfaces
findings.consequent: perception of brightness
findings.quote: increasing the luminance of the room surfaces will increase the perception of brightness

findings.antecedent: choosing higher CCT light source or one with larger gamut area
findings.consequent: perception of brightness
findings.quote: choosing a higher CCT light source or one with a larger gamut area will increase the perception of brightness

findings.antecedent: balancing luminaire luminance and area to be perceived as sparkling
findings.consequent: brightness of the room
findings.quote: Balancing the luminance and area so that the bright patch on the luminaire is perceived as sparkling will also enhance the brightness of the room.

findings.antecedent: increasing luminaire luminance too much or making luminous element too large
findings.consequent: glaring perception, diminished room brightness
findings.quote: Increasing the luminance further so that the luminaire becomes glaring will diminish the brightness of the room.

findings.antecedent: light source spectrum and luminance
findings.consequent: simple perception of color appearance
findings.quote: The simple perception of color appearance is linked to the spectrum of the light source and the luminance.

findings.antecedent: space with many colored surfaces
findings.consequent: effect of light source choice on color appearance
findings.quote: How strong an effect the choice of light source has depends on whether the space is essentially achromatic or one containing many colored surfaces. The effect of light source will be much greater for the latter conditions than the former...

findings.antecedent: higher-order perceptions (formality, spaciousness, complexity)
findings.consequent: less certain effect from luminous environment
findings.quote: The effect of the luminous environment on higher-order perceptions is much less certain. This is because higher-order perceptions, such as formality, are influenced by the whole of the environment, not just the luminous environment, as well as the context of the space and the culture of the observer.

findings.antecedent: average illuminance on working plane (500lx)
findings.consequent: satisfaction with office lighting
findings.quote: The illuminance on the working plane is a major determinant of satisfaction with the lighting in an office. There is support from a number of sources for the current average illuminance recommendation for offices in North America and Europe of about 500lx on the task.

findings.antecedent: daylighting (if carefully designed)
findings.consequent: good visibility for task/space, environmental stimulation (variation)
findings.quote: Daylight always deserves consideration because people like it, as long as it does not cause them thermal or visual discomfort. People like it because, if carefully designed, daylighting fully reveals both the task and the space and provides environmental stimulation by meaningful variation of lighting conditions.

findings.antecedent: electric lighting installations
findings.consequent: good visibility for task, rarely environmental stimulation
findings.quote: By comparison, electric lighting installations usually provide just good visibility for the task and rarely provide any environmental stimulation.

findings.antecedent: fluorescent lamp with high CIE general CRI (>80)
findings.consequent: easy performance of tasks requiring fine color discrimination, important color differences, or accurate color naming
findings.quote: The most universal answer is a fluorescent lamp with a high CIE general CRI (80). Such a lamp ensures that tasks that require fine color discrimination, or tasks where the color differences are important, or tasks where the accurate naming of colors is important can all be done easily.

findings.antecedent: light source with scotopically enriched spectrum
findings.consequent: performance of achromatic task (close to threshold) due to spectrum-induced decrease in pupil size
findings.quote: There is evidence that a light source with a scotopically enriched spectrum can enhance the performance of an achromatic task when the task is close to threshold, due to the spectrum-induced decrease in pupil size, but the effect disappears in suprathreshold conditions.

findings.antecedent: CRI >65 and nominally white color appearance
findings.consequent: lamp color properties as minor factor in satisfaction with office lighting
findings.quote: lamp color properties are a minor factor in determining the satisfaction felt with the lighting of an office. The illuminance provided is much more important.

findings.antecedent: light source color moves too far from people's expectations
findings.consequent: complaints
findings.quote: If the light source color moves too far from what peoples’ expectations are, it is likely that complaints will be heard.

findings.antecedent: average daylight factor >5%
findings.consequent: office perceived as daylit, electric lighting not needed daytime
findings.quote: any office where the average daylight factor is more than 5 percent will be perceived as daylit and the electric lighting will not be needed during the daytime.

findings.antecedent: average daylight factor <2%
findings.consequent: space perceived as electrically lit (even daytime), daylight only noticeable near windows
findings.quote: any space where the average daylight factor is significantly less than 2 percent, will be perceived as electrically lit, even in daytime (CIBSE, 2002a) and daylight will only be noticeable on room surfaces close to the windows.

findings.antecedent: conventional window
findings.consequent: provides daylight and view-out, but daylight decreases dramatically with distance from window
findings.quote: Windows have the advantage of providing both daylight to the interior and a view-out. Their disadvantage is that the amount of daylight delivered to the office decreases dramatically as the distance from the window increases...

findings.antecedent: direct, indirect, or direct/indirect electric lighting systems
findings.consequent: no feature always excludes one from consideration (depends on implementation)
findings.quote: there is no feature of direct, indirect, or direct/indirect lighting that always excludes it from consideration.

findings.antecedent: VDT luminaires (restricted luminances above certain angles)
findings.consequent: minimize reflected images on computer displays
findings.quote: The introduction of large numbers of computers into offices has led to the design of a class of luminaires with restricted luminances above certain angles, known as VDT luminaires. These luminaires are designed to minimize the number and magnitude of reflected images seen in the computer displays standing on desks.

findings.antecedent: modern display technology (high luminance background, low diffuse/specular reflectances)
findings.consequent: less need for special VDT luminaires
findings.quote: Modern display technology is becoming less sensitive to the ambient lighting conditions. This is particularly so when the display has a high luminance background and the screen on which the display is presented has low diffuse and specular reflectances.

findings.antecedent: windows with direct view of Sun
findings.consequent: should always be fitted with blinds
findings.quote: windows where a direct view of the Sun is possible should always be fitted with blinds of some sort.

findings.antecedent: manual lighting controls (simple, located where effect is visible)
findings.consequent: increased use by occupants
findings.quote: To ensure manual lighting controls will be used, keep them simple and located where the person using the controls can see what effect they have.

findings.antecedent: automatic electric lighting control systems (time switches, photosensor dimming, occupancy sensors)
findings.consequent: potential to eliminate energy waste
findings.quote: All three forms have the potential to eliminate energy waste by minimizing the use of electric lighting.

findings.antecedent: automatic electric lighting control systems (automatic operation, no manual override, no explanation)
findings.consequent: risk of complaints or sabotage
findings.quote: The problem with them all is that they are automatic and therefore do not take into account the vagaries of human nature and office life. Automatic electric lighting control systems should be like the perfect butler; they should perform without being noticed. The closer any specific system gets to this ideal, the more likely it is to be acceptable to the occupants of the office.

findings.antecedent: industrial lighting
findings.consequent: must be tailored to specific application due to variability in visual information, materials, environmental conditions
findings.quote: This variability means that good industrial lighting is inevitably tailored to the application.

findings.antecedent: industrial lighting
findings.consequent: facilitate quick/accurate work, contribute to safety, create comfortable visual environment
findings.quote: the objectives of industrial are the same everywhere. They are to facilitate quick and accurate work; to contribute to the safety of those doing the work and to create a comfortable visual environment.

findings.antecedent: minimum illuminances
findings.consequent: safe movement
findings.quote: Minimum illuminances are recommended for safe movement but illuminance alone is not enough.

findings.antecedent: disability glare, strong shadows, stroboscopic effect, poor color naming of safety colors
findings.consequent: safety
findings.quote: Care needs to be taken to avoid disability glare and strong shadows. Light sources should also be chosen to make the correct naming of safety colors easy. Where rotating or reciprocating machinery is in use, care should be taken to minimize any stroboscopic effect.

findings.antecedent: industrial lighting installations
findings.consequent: often less comfortable than office lighting
findings.quote: Many aspects of the physical environment are less comfortable in industry than in offices and lighting is often one of them.

findings.antecedent: lighting for visual inspection (off-axis detection of defects)
findings.consequent: depends on visibility/conspicuity of defect and other objects in search area
findings.quote: Rapid visual inspection calls for off-axis detection of defects. How well this can be done will depend on the visibility of the defect and, if there are other objects in the area to be searched, the conspicuity of the defect.

findings.antecedent: escape lighting (defined escape routes, electrical power absent/smoke present)
findings.consequent: safe and quick movement
findings.quote: Lighting designed to tell occupants which way to go and to illuminate the escape route so that people can move quickly and safely along it when electrical power is absent and/or smoke is present, is an important component of emergency egress systems.

findings.antecedent: exit sign of color
findings.consequent: enhanced conspicuity relative to other nominally white luminaires
findings.quote: The value of having an exit sign of color is that it enhances the conspicuity of the sign relative to other nominally white luminaires that may be operating at the same time.

findings.antecedent: green, luminous letters/symbols on black, opaque background (stencil sign format)
findings.consequent: most effective color and format for an exit sign (especially in smoke)
findings.quote: green, luminous letters or symbols on a black, opaque background is the most effective color and format for an exit sign. This stencil sign format will also be more effective in smoke than other formats...

findings.antecedent: low-mounted path-marking systems (in smoke)
findings.consequent: more effective in facilitating movement along escape route than wall/ceiling-mounted systems
findings.quote: In smoke, the low-mounted path-marking systems are more effective in facilitating movement along an escape route than the wall- or ceiling-mounted systems, provided the path-marking system has sufficient light output to provide an illuminance on the escape route of at least 0.1 lx.

findings.antecedent: current escape lighting practice
findings.consequent: often falls far short of good quality, provides false sense of security
findings.quote: While what is needed to provide good quality escape lighting is fairly well understood, what is offered in practice often falls far short... In many ways, current escape lighting practice provides a false sense of security.

findings.antecedent: road lighting
findings.consequent: useful accident countermeasure (especially for pedestrian fatalities at night)
findings.quote: The value of light as an accident countermeasure has been established for fatal accidents involving pedestrians at night, where the low visibility of the pedestrian is a contributory factor in the accident.

findings.antecedent: light spectrum stimulating rod photoreceptors (mesopic conditions)
findings.consequent: shorter reaction times and fewer misses for off-axis targets
findings.quote: Recent research has shown the light spectrum that effectively stimulates the rod photoreceptors of the retina will lead to shorter reaction times and fewer misses for off-axis targets than one that does not stimulate the rod photoreceptors, in mesopic conditions.

findings.antecedent: tunnel entrance seen as black-hole by approaching drivers (daytime)
findings.consequent: due to light scattered in the eye from surroundings
findings.quote: The black-hole effect is due to light scattered in the eye from the surroundings of the tunnel...

findings.antecedent: drivers entering tunnel find themselves misadapted (daytime)
findings.consequent: black-out effect
findings.quote: the black-out effect is due to the driver having insufficient time to adapt to the much lower luminances in the tunnel.

findings.antecedent: appropriate construction of tunnel entrance and grading of luminances
findings.consequent: overcome black-hole and black-out effects
findings.quote: Both these problems can be overcome by appropriate construction of the tunnel entrance and by following the recommendations for grading the luminances from the entrance to the interior of the tunnel.

findings.antecedent: traffic signals and changeable message signs
findings.consequent: must be bright enough to be conspicuous and legible by day, but not glare sources by night
findings.quote: Both traffic signals and changeable message signs have to be designed so that they are bright enough to be conspicuous and legible by day, but not so bright that they become glare sources by night.

findings.antecedent: rain (changing road surface reflection properties from diffuse to specular)
findings.consequent: less uniform road surface luminance, greater disability glare from vehicle forward lighting
findings.quote: Rain has its main effect by changing the reflection properties of the road surface from diffuse to specular, thereby making the luminance of the road surface provided by road lighting less uniform and the disability glare from vehicle forward lighting greater.

findings.antecedent: fog (multiple scattering of light)
findings.consequent: luminous veil, reduced luminance contrast, reduced visibility
findings.quote: Fog has its effect by multiple scattering of light, thereby producing a luminous veil that reduces the luminance contrast of everything ahead of the driver.

findings.antecedent: snow (backscattering incident light, individual flakes seen as visual noise)
findings.consequent: distraction to driver
findings.quote: Snow backscatters incident light and, provided each flake is seen as an individual item, creates a lot of visual noise in the driver’s visual field. How distracting this visual noise is depends on the luminance contrast of the snowflakes.

findings.antecedent: lighting
findings.consequent: crime prevention
findings.quote: lighting, per se, does not have a direct effect on the level of crime. Rather, lighting can affect crime by two indirect mechanisms.

findings.antecedent: increased surveillance (perceived by criminals as increasing effort/risk, decreasing reward)
findings.consequent: reduced incidence of crime
findings.quote: If such increased surveillance is perceived by criminals as increasing the effort and risk and decreasing the reward for a criminal activity, then the incidence of crime is likely to be reduced.

findings.antecedent: better lighting (more light sources, higher output, better color rendering, closer spaced)
findings.consequent: reduced levels of crime
findings.quote: better lighting usually involves the use of more light sources with higher light output and better color rendering, more closely spaced.

findings.antecedent: lighting (public pedestrianized areas: mean illuminance 10–50 lx, uniformity <15/1, glare ratio <4, good color rendering)
findings.consequent: detect and recognize threatening situations, provide accurate information about perpetrators
findings.quote: Lighting meeting this specification should allow anyone on the street to detect and recognize a threatening situation while there is still time to do something about it, and any witnesses to provide accurate information about the perpetrators.

findings.antecedent: CCTV cameras (limited dynamic range)
findings.consequent: best images when luminance range limited and shadows avoided
findings.quote: CCTV cameras all have a limited dynamic range so they provide the best images when the range of luminances in their field of view is limited and shadows are avoided on significant features, such as faces.

findings.antecedent: increasing age
findings.consequent: diminished ability to focus close up, reduced light to retina, increased scattered light, changed light spectrum, increased straylight
findings.quote: As the visual system ages, a number of changes in its structure and capabilities occur. With increasing years the ability to focus close up is diminished, the amount of light reaching the retina is reduced, more of the light reaching the retina is scattered, the spectrum of the light reaching the retina is changed and more straylight is generated inside the eye.

findings.antecedent: old age
findings.consequent: reduced absolute sensitivity to light, reduced visual acuity, reduced contrast sensitivity, reduced color discrimination, greater sensitivity to glare
findings.quote: At the threshold level, old age is characterized by reduced absolute sensitivity to light, reduced visual acuity, reduced contrast sensitivity, reduced color discrimination, and greater sensitivity to glare.

findings.antecedent: low vision (cataract, macular degeneration, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy)
findings.consequent: specific visual difficulties (e.g., seeing in dim light, reading small print, distinguishing dark colors)
findings.quote: Outside the laboratory, the elderly have difficulty with seeing in dim light, moving from bright to dark conditions suddenly, reading small print and distinguishing dark colors.

findings.antecedent: increasing luminance contrast of task details, making task details bigger, using more saturated colors
findings.consequent: visually easier tasks for elderly
findings.quote: The tasks they have difficulty with can be redesigned to make them visually easier. This usually involves increasing the luminance contrast of the task details, making the task details bigger and using more saturated colors.

findings.antecedent: higher illuminances (for elderly)
findings.consequent: benefit
findings.quote: The elderly benefit more from higher illuminances than do the young, but simply providing more light may not be enough.

findings.antecedent: lighting (disability/discomfort glare controlled, veiling reflections avoided)
findings.consequent: compensation for aging vision
findings.quote: The light has to be provided in such a way that both disability and discomfort glare are carefully controlled and veiling reflections are avoided.

findings.antecedent: transition zone (gradually reducing illuminance) when moving from well-lit to dark area (for elderly)
findings.consequent: visual system more time to adapt
findings.quote: Where elderly people are likely to be moving from a well-lit area to a dark area, a transition zone with a gradually reducing illuminance is desirable. Such a transition zone allows their visual system more time to make the necessary change in adaptation.

findings.antecedent: simplifying visual environment, attaching high luminance contrast to salient details (for low vision)
findings.consequent: generally useful approach
findings.quote: However, there is one approach which is generally useful. This approach is to simplify the visual environment and to make its salient details more visible by attaching high luminance contrast to those details, and only to those details.

findings.antecedent: sufficient doses of UV/visible/IR radiation
findings.consequent: tissue damage (eye/skin) via thermal/photochemical mechanisms
findings.quote: In sufficient doses, exposure to light can cause damage to both the eye and skin, through both thermal and photochemical mechanisms.

findings.antecedent: UV radiation
findings.consequent: photokeratitis of eye, erythema of skin, cataract in lens, skin aging, skin cancer
findings.quote: In the short term, UV radiation can cause photokeratitis of the eye and erythema of the skin. Prolonged exposure to UV radiation can lead to cataract in the lens as well as skin aging and skin cancer.

findings.antecedent: visible radiation
findings.consequent: photoretinitis of retina
findings.quote: Visible radiation can produce photoretinitis of the retina.

findings.antecedent: visible and short-wavelength IR radiation
findings.consequent: thermal damage to retina, burns to skin
findings.quote: Visible and short-wavelength IR radiation can cause thermal damage to the retina and burns to the skin.

findings.antecedent: prolonged exposure to IR radiation
findings.consequent: cataract and burns
findings.quote: Prolonged exposure to IR radiation can lead to cataract and burns.

findings.antecedent: most light sources (general lighting), evaluated against threshold limit values
findings.consequent: pose no hazard to health
findings.quote: When evaluated according to these threshold limit values, most light sources used for general lighting pose no hazard to health, but a few do.

findings.antecedent: sun
findings.consequent: most hazardous light source (for tissue damage)
findings.quote: The most hazardous light source to which most people are exposed is the sun.

findings.antecedent: newborn, aphakics, people taking certain pharmaceuticals
findings.consequent: more sensitive to light as radiation than normal population
findings.quote: Among such groups are the newborn, aphakics, and people taking certain pharmaceuticals. All these effects of light as radiation are negative but light as radiation can also have positive effects on health.

findings.antecedent: controlled exposure to light
findings.consequent: treatment for hyperbilirubinemia, some skin disorders, some tumors
findings.quote: Specifically, controlled exposure to light can be used as a treatment for hyperbilirubinemia, some skin disorders, and some tumors.

findings.antecedent: lighting conditions causing visual discomfort
findings.consequent: eyestrain
findings.quote: Lighting conditions that cause visual discomfort are likely to lead to eyestrain and anyone who frequently experiences eyestrain is not enjoying the best of health.

findings.antecedent: migraineurs and autistics
findings.consequent: especially sensitive to temporal modulation of light
findings.quote: Migraineurs and autistics are two such groups. Both are sensitive to the temporal modulation of light.

findings.antecedent: exposure to bright light at right time
findings.consequent: treatment for sleep disorders (timing and duration)
findings.quote: exposure to bright light at the right time can be used to treat some sleep disorders involving the timing and duration of sleep.

findings.antecedent: exposure to bright light
findings.consequent: stabilizing rest-activity cycle of Alzheimer's patients, relieving SAD symptoms
findings.quote: Exposure to bright light is also a useful means of stabilizing the rest-activity cycle of people with Alzheimer’s disease and of relieving the symptoms of seasonal affective disorder.

findings.antecedent: UV radiation
findings.consequent: destroy viruses, bacteria, molds, yeasts (purifier of air, liquids, granular materials)
findings.quote: UV radiation has been shown to destroy many species of bacteria, molds, yeasts, and viruses, many of which have the potential to damage human health.

findings.antecedent: lighting recommendations (laws, regulations, codes, guides, practices)
findings.consequent: influence lighting installations
findings.quote: Lighting research enters the lives of most people through the medium of documents specifying the amount of light to be provided for different applications, and/or offering guidance on how to provide that light.

findings.antecedent: lighting recommendations
findings.consequent: not immutable, change over time/countries based on technical, economic, and social factors
findings.quote: The nature of published lighting advice has changed over the years, the number of criteria that have to be considered tending to increase and the values of those criteria changing, depending on technical and economic circumstances, and people’s expectations.

findings.antecedent: provision of lighting
findings.consequent: electricity consumption, chemical pollution, light pollution
findings.quote: The provision of lighting has consequences beyond the ability to see. Specifically, the provision of lighting requires the consumption of electricity and that implies the generation of pollution.

findings.antecedent: maximizing efficiency of lighting installations
findings.consequent: reduced electricity consumption, beneficial effect on chemical pollution
findings.quote: maximizing the efficiency of lighting installations and thereby reducing the electricity consumed to provide the desired lighting conditions, would have a beneficial effect on many aspects of chemical pollution.

findings.antecedent: low-pressure sodium lamps (for street lighting near observatories)
findings.consequent: effective in reducing light pollution (astronomers could filter out wavelengths)
findings.quote: One of the earliest attempts to do this involved the use of low-pressure sodium light sources for street lighting in cities adjacent to observatories. This approach was effective because astronomers could easily filter out the very limited range of wavelengths produced by the low-pressure sodium lamp.

findings.antecedent: full cut-off luminaires (zero luminous intensity above horizontal)
findings.consequent: effective in reducing light trespass, less effective in reducing sky glow
findings.quote: Following this advice will certainly be effective in reducing light trespass, it may be less effective in reducing sky glow, for two reasons.

findings.antecedent: limiting amount of light used outdoors at night, limiting hours lighting is available
findings.consequent: successful long-term reduction of light pollution
findings.quote: The only approaches to reducing light pollution that are likely to be successful long term are those of limiting the amount of light used outdoors at night and of limiting the hours for which such lighting is available.

findings.antecedent: commercial imperative (e.g., petrol stations competing for brightness)
findings.consequent: escalating illuminances, increased light pollution
findings.quote: The power of this commercial imperative is evident in what has happened to the lighting of petrol stations in America. Over the last decade, a brightness war has broken out, the apparent aim being to have the brightest under-canopy lighting in the local market.

findings.antecedent: future lighting research (putting people first, accepting context, new approaches/measures)
findings.consequent: fruitful outcomes
findings.quote: On a philosophical level, these actions involve putting people before lighting and accepting the importance of context. On a technical level, they involve developing new approaches to the study of lighting, and new measures to quantify the magnitude of the visual component and how easy things are to see. On a practical level, they involve applying these approaches and measures to areas of interest, a number of which are suggested.

findings.antecedent: lighting
findings.consequent: aid to productivity, reduced energy consumption, enhanced health, improved quality of life
findings.quote: The most widely recognized “ends” are increasing productivity, reducing energy consumption, enhancing health, and improving the quality of life.

synthesis_conclusions: The human visual system responds to electromagnetic radiation between 380 and 780 nm, with its spectral sensitivity standardized by CIE Photopic and Scotopic Observers, allowing quantification of light (luminous flux, intensity, illuminance, luminance) and color (CCT, CRI).
Lighting metrics are precise but approximate the complex and individual visual effects, requiring a nuanced understanding of their application.
The visual system adapts to a wide range of luminances (photopic, mesopic, scotopic states), with fine discrimination in photopic conditions and reduced capabilities in scotopic conditions.
Perceptual constancies (lightness, color, size, shape) maintain stable object perception under varying lighting, but can break down with restricted or misleading information.

The human circadian system is entrained by the light-dark cycle, with light exposure timing and amount influencing phase shifts and immediate alertness, though its spectral sensitivity differs from the visual system.

Lighting conditions affect task performance through visual, circadian, and perceptual systems, with increasing illuminance generally improving visual performance with diminishing returns, but not overcoming inherent task difficulty.
Prolonged work in inappropriate lighting can lead to fatigue and mood changes, which can impact task performance.

Visual discomfort is caused by task difficulty, under/over-stimulation, distraction, and perceptual confusion, manifesting as physical symptoms (eyestrain, headaches) and influenced by factors like light quantity, uniformity, glare, veiling reflections, shadows, and flicker.

The perception of brightness is linked to luminance, light distribution, luminaire luminance, and light spectrum, with higher CCT and gamut area increasing perceived brightness, while excessive luminaire luminance can cause glare and diminish brightness.
Higher-order perceptions (formality, spaciousness, complexity) are less reliably influenced by lighting alone, depending more on context, past experience, and culture.
Office lighting must accommodate both self-luminous (VDT) and reflected light tasks, with 500lx being a common recommendation, but comfort also requires considering discomfort factors.

Daylighting is desired for visibility and environmental stimulation, but electric lighting is necessary due to daylight variability. Fluorescent lamps with high CRI (>80) are generally suitable, but specific preferences vary by culture and context.
Modern VDT technology reduces the need for specialized VDT luminaires, but window blinds and simple, visible manual controls are crucial for occupant satisfaction and energy saving.

Industrial lighting must be tailored to diverse visual tasks and environmental constraints, aiming for quick/accurate work, safety, and comfort, with attention to illuminance, glare, shadows, and color rendering for safety colors.

Escape lighting is critical for safe evacuation, with colored, luminous stencil exit signs on dark backgrounds being most effective, especially in smoke. Low-mounted path-marking is superior in smoke to ceiling-mounted systems.
Current escape lighting practice often falls short of good quality and maintenance, providing a false sense of security.

Road lighting enhances driving safety, particularly for pedestrians at night, with light spectrum influencing off-axis detection in mesopic conditions. Tunnel lighting requires specific design to counter black-hole and black-out effects.

Traffic signals and changeable message signs need to be conspicuous and legible by day without causing glare at night. Adverse weather (rain, fog, snow) significantly degrades visibility, requiring specific lighting and road material considerations.

Lighting indirectly reduces crime by facilitating surveillance and enhancing community confidence, with specific illuminance, uniformity, glare control, and color rendering recommendations for public areas.
CCTV systems require limited luminance ranges and shadow avoidance for optimal image quality.

Aging causes structural and functional changes in the visual system (reduced focus, light to retina, acuity, contrast sensitivity, color discrimination, increased glare sensitivity), leading to difficulties in dim light, small print, and dark colors.

Compensation for aging vision involves lenses, task redesign (larger, higher contrast, saturated colors), higher illuminances, and careful glare/reflection control, with transition zones for dark adaptation.

Light as radiation can cause tissue damage (photokeratitis, erythema, cataract, skin cancer, photoretinitis, burns) from UV, visible, and IR exposure, but controlled exposure can also treat conditions like hyperbilirubinemia, skin disorders, and tumors.
Exposure to bright light at appropriate times can treat sleep disorders and stabilize rest-activity cycles in Alzheimer's patients, and UV radiation can purify air/liquids/materials.

Lighting recommendations are dynamic, consensus-based, and influenced by technology, economics, and societal expectations, highlighting the need for thoughtful application rather than rigid adherence.

Lighting's broader consequences include electricity consumption (leading to chemical pollution) and light pollution (sky glow, light trespass), which require energy efficiency, careful luminaire design, and limiting outdoor light use/hours.
evidence_gaps: A new “Standard Circadian Observer” is needed before the effects of different spectral power distributions on the circadian system can be evaluated.

Quantitative predictions of lighting effects on visual performance for all tasks are not yet possible, especially for tasks not dominated by the visual component, requiring visual search, or falling outside the RVP model's development ranges.
A task analysis procedure is needed to determine the relative impacts of visual and non-visual components on task performance to extend the RVP model.
More data are needed before a model of visual performance covering visual search can be constructed.
A measure of how easy a target is to see, including both lighting and target characteristics in one metric, is needed.
A more precise estimate of the magnitude of the visual component in work tasks is needed, potentially through eye movement recording and restricted viewing time.
More studies are needed to examine different contexts for lighting's effect on impression and behavior to formulate general rules.
A plausible mechanism for discomfort glare is not yet identified.
The extent to which UV exposure is an important factor for chronic cataract development needs to be resolved.
Comprehensive epidemiological studies examining the link between light exposure history and retinal deterioration with age are needed.
The absolute sensitivity of the circadian system to a given spectrum delivered at the eye for a fixed time needs to be identified for sleep disorder treatment.
The cause of winter SAD is unknown, and explanations based on circadian system disturbances or serotonin regulation are unproven.

More research is needed on how lighting distributions that do not affect task visibility or cause visual discomfort might affect mood and motivation of office workers or alter the 'message' sent by lighting.
The extent to which the advantage of metal halide lighting in mesopic conditions would decline if the scene was essentially achromatic remains to be determined.
The validity of the physiological model for visual clarity needs to be tested on independent data.
The conflict about photoreceptors and perceptions in visual clarity needs to be resolved to construct suitable predictive models.
More research is needed on how and why different light spectra affect the perception of brightness of interiors.
Urgent measurements of the state of adaptation of the visual system while driving at night in different lighting conditions are needed.
The will to consider all components involved in making an object visible to the driver in all conditions is missing in road lighting design.
The extent to which low illuminance and light spectra findings on safety color naming are due to each factor remains to be determined.
It is unclear whether the effect of light spectrum on brightness would be more pronounced in areas with varied colors (e.g., parks) than achromatic ones.
The extent to which the minimum glazing transmittance would increase or decrease with longer exposures (sensitization vs. habituation) is unknown.
The effects of latitude on minimum acceptable glazing transmittance are matters of conjecture.
The effect of illuminance uniformity on visibility in smoke has not been methodically studied.
The specific smoke density that people can survive for a brief time is not simply answered.
The relative impact of different entraining stimuli (light, social cues, activity) and how they interact is unknown for the circadian system.
Long-term side-effects produced by manipulation of the circadian system need to be understood.
The links between changes in physiology following light exposure and effects on task performance in realistic conditions need better appreciation.
The general standard of exterior lighting could be better, and greater knowledge of how people respond to lighting will aid and encourage better practice.
Industrial lighting research needs to develop different approaches for factories, as current data is often based on office work.
An understanding of how lighting might be used in retail situations to influence sales and behavior is of considerable interest.
The validity of the luminance uniformity criterion used in roadway lighting needs to be re-evaluated.
The validity of the argument that light emitted close to the horizontal produces more sky glow than light emitted vertically upward needs to be tested.

publication_bias: Not applicable for a textbook/narrative review.
limitations: Many lighting metrics are precise but inaccurate for quantifying the visual effect due to the complexity and flexibility of the human visual system and individual differences.
Generalizing findings from specific real-task studies is difficult due to the unique balance of visual, cognitive, and motor components in each task.

The RVP model is applicable to a limited range of tasks (visual-dominated, foveal vision, fully characterized stimuli) and requires further development for tasks with significant non-visual components or peripheral vision.
Visual discomfort is highly individual and context-dependent, making universal criteria challenging.
The link between luminous environment and perception is tenuous, influenced by adaptation, background, past experience, and knowledge.
Higher-order perceptions (formality, spaciousness, complexity) are less reliably influenced by simple lighting variables and depend heavily on context and culture.
The effectiveness of lighting recommendations is limited by their consensus-based nature, technical feasibility, economic viability, and the need to balance conflicting aims.
The impact of light on health is complex, with potential positive and negative effects depending on dose, wavelength, exposure duration, and individual sensitivity.

The effectiveness of light-based interventions (e.g., for circadian rhythms, SAD) can be difficult to achieve in real-world contexts due to compliance issues and the need for comprehensive control over light exposure.
The components of lighting systems for driving have been developed piecemeal, often without considering their combined effects or the full range of conditions drivers experience.
The effectiveness of crime prevention lighting is indirect, relying on surveillance and community confidence, and can be undermined by criminal perceptions or other influences.
